stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli, 19, Wins Monaco Grand Prix, Becomes Youngest Winner in Race History
stories.summary:
Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes won the Monaco Grand Prix on Sunday, setting a record as the youngest driver ever to win the prestigious street race. The 19-year-old Italian, who replaced seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton at Mercedes this season, now has five consecutive race victories and leads the Formula 1 championship standings by 66 points over Hamilton.

The race was disrupted midway through when sections of the Monaco circuit's asphalt broke apart, triggering a red flag after two cars crashed, including Charles Leclerc's Ferrari. After a lengthy delay, officials restarted the race from a standing start — a rare occurrence at Monaco — and Antonelli controlled the restart to seal the win.

Hamilton finished second and offered generous praise for his successor. "He's only 19, so just imagine what the future holds for him," Hamilton said after the race. "It's a real privilege to witness it." Max Verstappen, the four-time defending champion, retired on the first lap after losing power at the start.

Antonelli's rapid ascent has reshaped the 2026 championship picture entirely. His teammate George Russell dropped out of the top 10 with a penalty, his second consecutive poor result, further cementing Antonelli's commanding position in the standings with the season still in its early stages.

stories.headline: Trump Declines to Rule Out Payments to Jan. 6 Rioters Who Attacked Police, Even as DOJ Shelves Anti-Weaponization Fund
stories.summary:
President Trump said in a Sunday interview on NBC News's "Meet the Press" that he would not rule out compensating individuals who were charged with assaulting police officers during the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, saying "I have to see it" when pressed directly. Trump defended the administration's short-lived "anti-weaponization" fund — a nearly $1.8 billion proposal — calling it "a great idea," even though acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Friday that the fund would not move forward.

The remarks came despite bipartisan criticism. Former Vice President Mike Pence condemned the pardons for January 6 rioters and said they should not receive compensation for their actions. Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) has signaled support for alternative mechanisms, and legal analysts note the DOJ retains other pathways — including the Federal Tort Claims Act — that could be used to make payouts to those who claim they were wronged by the government.

Supporters of the fund argue it was necessary to address what they call the politicized prosecution of Trump allies during the Biden administration. Critics, including Democrats and some Republicans, say compensating individuals convicted of attacking law enforcement officers would be an unprecedented misuse of taxpayer funds and a signal that political violence carries no lasting consequence.

The episode highlights an ongoing tension within the administration over how far to go in rehabilitating January 6 participants. With the fund formally shelved, attention now turns to whether the DOJ will pursue alternative legal channels to deliver compensation, and whether Congress will act on related proposals.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Explores Purchasing Chagos Islands to Secure Diego Garcia Military Base
stories.summary:
The Trump administration is reportedly considering a U.S. purchase of the Chagos Islands in the Indian Ocean as an alternative to a British plan to transfer sovereignty of the archipelago to Mauritius, according to a report published Sunday by the Telegraph. The move would be aimed at securing long-term American control of the Diego Garcia military base, one of the Pentagon's most strategically significant overseas installations, which has served as a hub for bomber operations, naval assets, and intelligence missions for decades.

A 2025 agreement negotiated by British Prime Minister Keir Starmer would have transferred sovereignty to Mauritius while allowing the U.S. and U.K. to continue operating the Diego Garcia base under a 99-year lease. Trump initially appeared open to the deal before publicly calling the transfer "great stupidity" and urging Starmer not to "give away Diego Garcia." U.S. officials are also reportedly wary of Mauritius's ties to Iran and China. Britain subsequently shelved the legislation needed to ratify the sovereignty transfer.

Diego Garcia played a central role in recent U.S. military operations during the conflict with Iran, with long-range aircraft and logistical assets operating from the island. The prospect of a direct U.S. purchase would be an extraordinary and historically novel diplomatic move, raising questions about international law, the rights of the Chagossian people who were displaced from the islands decades ago, and the future of the U.S.-U.K. alliance framework.

The White House had not responded to requests for comment as of the time of reporting. The proposal remains at the discussion stage among administration officials, and no formal offer has been made.

stories.headline: Federal Lawsuit Seeks to Block UFC Fight at the White House Scheduled for Trump's 80th Birthday
stories.summary:
A federal lawsuit filed Saturday seeks to block a UFC fight card planned for the White House South Lawn on June 14, President Trump's 80th birthday, which coincides with the nation's 250th anniversary. Plaintiffs' attorneys argue the event is "deeply corrupt" and that Trump is unlawfully benefiting from it financially, citing reports that he purchased a stake in UFC. The lawsuit contends the administration did not obtain proper approvals for a commercial fighting event on federal property.

The UFC event is one of the most prominent commercial spectacles ever staged at the White House, and it has drawn scrutiny over the blurring of presidential duties with private business interests. The White House has not publicly addressed the lawsuit. The event is expected to draw significant crowds and media attention as part of broader birthday and national anniversary celebrations.

Critics, primarily from the left, argue the event represents an unprecedented use of public grounds for private commercial gain and sets a troubling precedent for presidential self-dealing. Supporters contend the administration has broad authority over White House grounds and that the event is a legitimate celebration of both a national milestone and the president's birthday, with no impropriety in Trump's business ties.

A federal judge in Washington, D.C. had separately dismissed an unrelated lawsuit by the Kennedy Center against a jazz musician last week. Whether a judge will act on the UFC lawsuit before the June 14 date remains to be seen.

stories.headline: Update: Bill Pulte Appointment as Acting DNI Threatens FISA Reauthorization, Top Democrat Warns
stories.summary:
Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said Sunday that President Trump's decision to appoint Bill Pulte as acting Director of National Intelligence is likely the most dangerous of Trump's intelligence-community appointments and has effectively taken FISA Section 702 reauthorization "off the table." Himes made the remarks on CBS News's "Face the Nation," warning that Pulte's confirmation prospects and political profile make bipartisan cooperation on spy-powers renewal nearly impossible.

Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which authorizes warrantless surveillance of foreign targets and is a cornerstone of U.S. counterterrorism and counterintelligence operations, requires periodic congressional reauthorization. Democrats and some Republicans have long conditioned their support for renewal on executive-branch commitments to oversight and civil-liberties protections. Himes argued that Pulte, who has no intelligence background, undermines that prospect.

The Trump administration has not publicly responded to Himes's specific remarks. Republicans have generally backed the appointment, arguing the president is entitled to place trusted loyalists atop the intelligence community. The dispute adds to broader congressional tensions over the administration's handling of the nation's intelligence apparatus.

stories.headline: DHS Says Commissary Data Undercuts Delaney Hall Hunger Strike Claims
stories.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security has released commissary revenue data from the Delaney Hall immigration detention center in Newark, N.J., asserting that the figures contradict Democratic lawmakers' accounts of an ongoing hunger strike among detainees. According to DHS, weekly commissary sales at the facility nearly tripled — rising from roughly $11,500 to more than $30,000 — during the period when the hunger strike was reported to be in effect, even as the detainee population fell by about 14 percent.

DHS Deputy Press Secretary Lauren Bis characterized the strike as a "hoax," suggesting detainees were skipping institutional meals in favor of snack items purchased from the commissary. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who testified before Congress on the matter, said some of the dispute stemmed from detainees objecting to Americanized food that did not reflect their home-country cuisines.

Democratic members of Congress from New Jersey, including Sen. Andy Kim and Reps. Robert Menendez Jr. and Bonnie Watson-Coleman, had toured the facility and said detainee accounts of poor conditions, moldy food, and medical neglect were credible. Advocacy group Cosecha and detainees' handwritten letters alleged overcrowding, lack of air conditioning, and denial of medication. The competing claims have made Delaney Hall a focal point in the broader national debate over immigration detention standards and the Trump administration's enforcement policies.

stories.headline: California Primary Results: Multiple Congressional and Statewide Races Decided
stories.summary:
California held its 2026 primary elections Sunday, with competitive House races across the state producing results that will shape the November midterm battlefield. Among the closely watched contests is the 47th Congressional District, where Republican Jenny Rae Le Roux is challenging Democratic incumbent Rep. Dave Min, and results in the 11th District are also being tabulated. California uses a top-two primary system in which the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advance to the general election.

The 2026 midterms carry significant stakes for control of the House of Representatives, which Republicans hold by a narrow margin. California is home to several competitive districts that analysts consider potential party-flip targets, and primary outcomes will determine which candidates — and which parties — appear on November ballots in key races. Record numbers of congressional retirements nationally have added volatility to the cycle.

Results were being reported live as counting continued. The outcomes of California's primaries are expected to clarify the midterm map and will be closely analyzed by both parties for signals about voter sentiment heading into the fall campaign.

stories.headline: Gunman Kills One, Wounds Five in Israel Before Being Shot Dead by Security Forces
stories.summary:
One person was killed and five others wounded Sunday when an Israeli Arab man opened fire at multiple locations near the town of Kokhav Yair in central Israel, close to the occupied West Bank. Israeli emergency service Magen David Adom said two of the wounded were in serious condition and three in moderate condition. Security forces killed the suspect, identified as an Israeli Arab with a prior criminal record, following a brief chase. A second suspect was arrested after making statements indicating involvement in the attack.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the attacker a "heinous terrorist" in remarks to his cabinet. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir invoked a recently passed Israeli law establishing the death penalty as the default sentence for Palestinians convicted of deadly terrorist attacks, saying it applied to Israeli Arab citizens as well and expressing satisfaction that the attacker was killed rather than captured.

Israeli forces subsequently closed two checkpoints near the northern West Bank city of Tulkarem and set up temporary checkpoints near Qalqilya following the attack. About one-fifth of Israeli citizens are Arab, and the incident reignites longstanding tensions over the legal and political status of Arab citizens within Israel, as well as the application of counterterrorism laws to that population.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Strikes Chornobyl Nuclear Facility as Zelensky Meets Western Allies in London
stories.summary:
A Russian drone struck a storage facility for spent nuclear fuel near the Chornobyl nuclear plant in northern Ukraine on Sunday, partially destroying a building and triggering a fire that was subsequently extinguished. Ukrainian nuclear operator Enerhoatom reported no injuries and said radiation levels remained stable, but condemned the attack as a deliberate threat to nuclear safety. President Volodymyr Zelensky called it a "vile" and deliberate strike on "extremely critical infrastructure," and detailed that Russia launched 88 missiles, more than 3,250 drones and 1,800 guided bombs over the past week across 13 regions.

The strike came as Zelensky traveled to London for talks at Downing Street with UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — the so-called E3 group and some of Kyiv's strongest allies. The meeting focused on European support for Ukraine and potential security guarantees as part of any future peace process. The gathering takes on added urgency after Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday rejected Zelensky's proposal for direct face-to-face negotiations, saying he saw no point in meeting the Ukrainian leader.

The London summit marks a new development in Western coordination at a moment when U.S. mediation efforts have stalled, with Washington's diplomatic attention largely shifted to the ongoing conflict with Iran. Ukraine separately struck St. Petersburg and its surroundings over the weekend in what Russian authorities described as an unprecedented drone attack, targeting the city during Putin's flagship economic forum. The Chornobyl attack drew immediate international condemnation given the site's history and the potential symbolic and physical risks of striking nuclear infrastructure.

stories.headline: Hundreds Freed from Boko Haram Mountain Hideout in Nigeria After Months of Captivity
stories.summary:
At least 360 people — and by some accounts as many as 416 — kidnapped by Boko Haram jihadists from the mainly Muslim community of Ngoshe in Nigeria's northeastern Borno state in March have been freed from a remote Mandara mountain hideout. Two infants died due to exhaustion from prolonged captivity and the harsh terrain, according to a senior adviser to President Bola Tinubu. The remaining captives are receiving medical care, and efforts are underway to locate others believed to have fled into Cameroon.

The Nigerian military said it carried out an intelligence-led night operation that took the militants by surprise, describing it as one of its "most significant hostage rescue operations" in the northeast. However, a local civil society group, the Borno South Youth Initiative, disputes that account, saying it brokered an unconditional release through direct mediation with the militants, placing the freed total at 416. The dispute over credit reflects ongoing tensions between government authorities and local intermediaries over how ransoms and negotiations are handled.

The mass abduction took place in early March as residents were breaking their Ramadan fast. Mass kidnappings for ransom have become widespread across Nigeria in recent years, carried out by various armed groups targeting schools, mosques and remote villages. Boko Haram's 2014 abduction of more than 200 Chibok schoolgirls — roughly 90 of whom remain missing — drew global attention to the tactic, which analysts say has been perpetuated by ransom payments that provide militants a continuing financial incentive.

stories.headline: Update: Platner Defiant as Collins Calls Abuse Allegations 'Troubling' Ahead of Maine Senate Primary
stories.summary:
Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner returned to the campaign trail Friday, declaring "Maine has my back" in defiance of mounting scrutiny over allegations published by The New York Times that multiple women who had romantic relationships with him described disturbing or intimidating behavior. The allegations have drawn a response from Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who called the latest claims "troubling" as voters prepare to head to the polls in the upcoming Senate primaries.

Platner, a progressive oyster farmer, is the presumptive Democratic nominee in what is expected to be a competitive general election race against Collins, one of the most closely watched Senate contests of the cycle. His campaign has pushed back against the reporting, with Platner suggesting the coverage has been politically motivated and that Maine voters will judge him on his record and platform.

The allegations add a significant complication to Democratic efforts to flip Collins's seat. Collins, who has served in the Senate since 1997 and is known for occasionally crossing party lines, framed the allegations as a character issue for voters to weigh. The episode echoes broader national conversations about vetting of candidates and the role of character allegations in competitive primaries.

stories.headline: Scott Pelley Says CBS Accused Him of Physically Abusing New '60 Minutes' Producer Before Firing
stories.summary:
Former CBS News correspondent Scott Pelley, a fixture on "60 Minutes" since 2004, says he was accused by CBS News President Tom Cibrowski of "physically abusing" newly appointed executive producer Nick Bilton before he was fired from the program. In an interview published Sunday by the New York Times, Pelley disputed the characterization and offered his account of his final days at the network, describing the accusation as the stated basis for his dismissal.

Pelley's departure comes during a period of significant transition at "60 Minutes," which recently came under the editorial direction of Bari Weiss, the journalist and founder of The Free Press who has been critical of mainstream media institutions. The leadership change has drawn both praise from conservatives who see it as a corrective to perceived liberal bias and concern from longtime CBS journalists who worry about the program's editorial independence.

The story has drawn coverage from outlets across the political spectrum, including the National Review and Washington Examiner on the right and the New York Times on the left, reflecting the broad interest in the future direction of one of American television's most storied news programs. Pelley's allegations of a pretextual firing add a new legal and reputational dimension to the already closely watched shakeup at CBS News.

stories.headline: Update: US-Iran War Expands as Ceasefire Talks Proceed, Iran Strikes Kuwait Bases
stories.summary:
The United States announced a ceasefire agreement Wednesday night following fresh talks, but strikes continued in the interim as both sides exchanged blows. Iran targeted US military bases in Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for American strikes on an Iranian oil tanker and island, while US forces struck Iranian drones and radar sites. One person was killed and more than 60 injured in an Iranian drone strike, and BBC Verify analysis found Iran has damaged 20 US military sites since the start of the conflict.

The ceasefire announcement comes amid what analysts describe as a tense cycle of negotiations, with President Trump repeatedly claiming progress. BBC Verify also found that Tehran's strikes were more extensive than publicly acknowledged, while satellite imagery confirmed significant damage at US-linked facilities. The Strait of Hormuz situation continues to weigh on some 20,000 seafarers trapped in the war zone.

The broader conflict continues to ripple through the region. Israel has warned it will resume striking the Lebanese capital as Hezbollah increasingly uses fiber-optic drones against Israeli soldiers and civilians, and Israeli forces are under investigation for a strike in south Lebanon. Meanwhile, neither side appears to want a return to all-out war, though the latest exchange of strikes underscores the fragility of diplomatic progress.

Iran's government has imposed an internet blackout since the start of hostilities in February, cutting most Iranians off from outside information. The war's economic toll on Iran is intensifying, with US officials claiming a military and economic advantage, though Iran continues to project defiance through ongoing strike operations.

stories.headline: Flesh-Eating Screwworm Found in Second Texas Calf; Canada Bans Texas Livestock Imports
stories.summary:
Canada's Food Inspection Agency announced a temporary ban on cattle and horses from Texas after the USDA confirmed a second screwworm case in a one-month-old calf in Zavala County, roughly 5.6 miles from the site of the first confirmed case. The second detection came within a 20-kilometer control zone established after the initial discovery, which marked the parasite's first appearance in Texas in 60 years. Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared a state of disaster on Friday, warning the outbreak "is likely to spread over the course of the summer."

The New World Screwworm is a parasitic fly whose larvae burrow through the living flesh of warm-blooded animals and humans, entering through wounds and mucous membranes and potentially killing the host if untreated. The outbreak is part of a broader infestation moving northward through Central America and Mexico, which has been under heavy surveillance by US agricultural authorities. Texas is the leading US beef and cattle producer, making the outbreak a significant threat to the national agricultural supply chain.

Canadian officials said the ban covers any livestock that was in Texas within 21 days of crossing the border. While they assessed the risk of establishment in Canada as low due to colder temperatures, they urged farmers to monitor livestock for wounds and advised travelers returning from Texas to check pets. The US and Canada conduct a substantial two-way cattle trade, with 550,000 head imported from the US in 2025 alone.

The USDA has enacted quarantines, movement controls, and expanded surveillance in the affected area. The parasite was considered eradicated in the US in 1966, though isolated cases have reappeared since, including an outbreak in the 1970s. Officials are racing to contain the current outbreak before warmer summer conditions allow the fly to spread more widely.

stories.headline: Update: More Than One Million Attend Pope Leo XIV's Open-Air Mass in Madrid
stories.summary:
More than one million people filled the streets of Madrid on Sunday as Pope Leo XIV celebrated an open-air mass in the Spanish capital, the second day of his official visit to Spain — the first papal trip to the country in 15 years. King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia were among the congregants, while crowds waved Spanish and Vatican flags and threw petals as the pope passed in his popemobile through the Plaza de Cibeles. In his sermon, the pontiff urged the faithful to see religion not as "a museum of the past" but as a living force for helping the poor and marginalized.

The visit follows a prayer vigil Saturday night near Real Madrid's Santiago Bernabeu stadium attended by approximately 500,000 people, most of them young. During a reception at the royal palace Saturday, the pope praised Spain's commitment to peace, its opposition to global conflicts, and its support for migrants. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a socialist who has clashed with President Trump over the US-Israel war with Iran and with Israel over Gaza, hosted the pontiff.

Pope Leo XIV, who was born in Chicago, has drawn criticism from President Trump over his anti-war positions. His remarks in Madrid echoed those tensions, praising Spain's "faithful adherence to international law." The trip is set to include an unprecedented address before the Spanish parliament and a meeting with survivors of sexual abuse within the Catholic Church.

Later in the week, the pope will travel with Prime Minister Sánchez to the Canary Islands to honor thousands of migrants who have died attempting to reach Europe. The visit carries both religious and geopolitical significance given the pope's public stances on immigration and international conflict.

stories.headline: Federal Regulators Sue Multiple States Over Efforts to Ban Prediction Markets
stories.summary:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has filed lawsuits against seven states — Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Wisconsin, Minnesota, New York, and Rhode Island — over their attempts to ban or restrict online prediction markets, setting up a major legal battle over whether such platforms are illegal gambling or federally regulated financial products. The CFTC has also intervened in related cases in Ohio, Massachusetts, and Nevada. The core legal question is whether the Commodity Exchange Act grants the federal government exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market contracts, or whether states retain authority to regulate what they characterize as gambling.

CFTC Chairman Michael Selig has argued that prediction markets, which allow users to trade on the outcomes of real-world events, fall squarely under federal oversight. "States cannot circumvent the clear directive of Congress," he said in announcing the Wisconsin lawsuit. Companies such as Kalshi and Polymarket, which have rapidly grown in prominence following high-profile use during the 2024 elections, stand to be directly affected by the outcome.

State officials are pushing back forcefully, with a bipartisan coalition of 41 state attorneys general writing to the CFTC arguing the agency lacks exclusive authority. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong called the federal position a recycling of "industry arguments that have been rejected in district courts across the country." Utah's Republican Governor Spencer Cox, whose state has a blanket gambling ban, vowed to use "every resource" to defeat the CFTC in court.

The dispute touches on broader questions about federalism and the evolution of financial technology. Multiple district courts have so far sided with state positions, though the CFTC's aggressive legal strategy suggests the issue will ultimately require appellate or Supreme Court resolution. The outcome could define the regulatory landscape for an industry that processed billions of dollars in contracts during the 2024 election cycle.
